articles.teaser: Democrats resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next yearSign up for the Breaking News US emailThe National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other, according to the New York Times.The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors.A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed.The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role.The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December. Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race.Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers.

articles.headline: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
articles.teaser: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young peopleThis should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s.

articles.headline: Here’s how we can give Neets a fighting chance | Letters
articles.teaser: Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s plan to tackle the youth jobs crisisWhy is Labour reinventing the wheel (Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people, 16 November)? There is an easier and less discriminatory way – and that is through the mainstream education system. This would not dump these young people into a post-16 Neet silo.Further education (FE) colleges have been working in the area of young people’s training and further education for decades. articles.headline: Save our streets from yet more advertising | Letter
articles.teaser: Reasons to refuse planning permission are limited to ‘public safety’ and ‘amenity’, writes James WardIn response to your report (Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank, 13 November) perhaps we could start with the harbinger of high-street decline, the digital advertising screen. You know the ones, the pavement-blocking LED monoliths, with screens on both sides broadcasting six ads per minute to passersby.Even as shops have shuttered, numbers of such ad machines skyrocketed 256% between 2018 and 2025. The ads shown are invariably for global mega-corporations, further driving commerce online, and for unhealthy products such as junk food, alcohol, gambling and vapes (although the latter are to be banned from 1 June 2027). At nearly 3 metres tall and 1.24 metres wide, they contribute to pavement clutter and disrupt sightlines of historic town centres.
articles.originalHeadline: Save our streets from yet more advertising | Letter

articles.headline: Another fine mess for the flag-botherers? | Letters
articles.teaser: Pam Stanier and Dr Chris Haughton on people who put up union flags and hang them upside downIt is surely ironic that the individuals who put up union flags frequently hang them upside down, as in your photo (‘Visceral response’: flag campaigns inspire anti-racism organising across England, 16 November). The broad white diagonal stripe should be at the top nearest the flagpole.Displaying the narrow stripe uppermost is widely considered a sign of distress. Which is what I feel when I see a street sullied by the flags, whether hung correctly or not. It is an aggressive display likely to lead to disunity, not what the “union” should mean at all.
articles.originalHeadline: Another fine mess for the flag-botherers? | Letters

articles.headline: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
articles.teaser: Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed courseworkIs this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them (Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November)? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt?We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device.
articles.originalHeadline: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter

But after some difficult weeks, our party needs an overhaulCaroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MPIn the aftermath of some difficult weeks for the Greens, one encouraging response has particularly stood out for me: the widespread agreement across progressive politics that the UK is better for having a strong Green party. One that will hold other parties to account for their delivery on social and environmental justice and that will put issues on the political agenda that other parties won’t.From Rosebank to wealth taxes and ending arms sales to Israel, Greens are stretching the Overton window so that the gap narrows between what’s necessary and what’s currently deemed politically acceptable. articles.teaser: In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting BrexitThis week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night, could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership.For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible.

articles.headline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
